The current healthcare Q&A matches suggest that differentiating between nonalcoholic and alcoholic steatohepatitis (ASH) using routine laboratory markers is not entirely accurate. While some markers like higher MCVs (mean corpuscular volume), AST/ALT ratios, and biomarkers like lipids may indicate liver disease, they do not reliably differentiate between the two conditions.

In fact, the matches imply that these biomarkers might be more useful in guiding selection of patients for a liver biopsy rather than distinguishing ASH from alcoholic hepatitis (ASH). Moreover, these markers may also fail to differentiate ASH from nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, as suggested by studies indicating higher MCVs and AST/ALT ratios in both conditions.

The matches also highlight the importance of considering other factors, such as clinical presentation, symptoms, and imaging findings, when making a diagnosis. Further research is recommended to better understand the relationship between biomarkers and liver disease severity, as well as to identify potential correlations with specific patient populations or risk factors.
